planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification into lean, rocky or gravelly, fast-draining soil in full sun; this Chihuahuan Desert mountain species resents heavy or constantly moist garden soil and establishes best where drainage mimics its native rocky slopes.

directions: Bigbend beebalm is a little-grown native perennial restricted to rocky canyons and dry slopes of the Chihuahuan Desert mountains of the Big Bend region of Texas, far southeastern New Mexico, and adjacent northern Mexico, where it grows at moderate elevation among limestone and igneous outcrops. Its pale lavender to pink tubular flowers cluster in tight terminal heads atop wiry stems in summer, and the foliage carries a sharp, oregano-like fragrance that becomes noticeable with the lightest touch. It is markedly more drought tolerant than the eastern garden bee balms and declines quickly if kept in rich, damp soil, performing best in the same lean, gritty conditions favored by desert penstemons and zinnias. In a rock garden or xeric border it draws native bees and occasional hummingbirds while needing essentially no irrigation once its roots are established.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or set out transplants in spring into thin, rocky limestone soil in partial shade to full sun; green bee balm grows naturally in the dappled light of Edwards Plateau oak-juniper woodlands and declines in deep shade or heavy, poorly drained ground.

directions: Green bee balm is a Texas Hill Country endemic restricted to the limestone canyons and oak-juniper woodlands of the Edwards Plateau, where thin rocky soils and part-day shade keep it cooler and drier than typical bee balm habitat. Its small summer flowers are an unusual pale greenish-white rather than the pink, red, or purple of most Monarda, giving the species its name, and they emerge from whorled bracts along slender upright stems above aromatic foliage. Because the species is considered rare in the wild, garden plantings grown from nursery seed or propagated stock help take pressure off native populations while still providing a genuine regional pollinator resource for small bees. It is best suited to a rock garden, limestone bed, or lightly shaded native planting with sharp drainage rather than a conventional moist perennial border.

common_name: Yellow Elder (Tropical Esperanza, Lluvia de Oro)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in full sun after all frost danger has passed; var. stans is the broad-leaflet tropical form of yellow bells and is noticeably less cold hardy than the narrow-leaf var. angustata, so it suits warm coastal and South Florida/Caribbean-climate gardens better than desert or inland sites.

directions: Tecoma stans var. stans is the broad-leaved, nominate tropical variety of yellow bells, native to South Florida, the Caribbean, and lowland Mexico and Central America, where it grows as a large multi-stemmed shrub or small tree rather than the more compact, narrow-leaflet desert form (var. angustata) grown in the Southwest. Its wider, glossier leaflets and vigorous, almost continuous production of golden trumpet flowers make it a striking specimen in frost-free or nearly frost-free landscapes, and in South Florida it is sometimes called by its Spanish name, lluvia de oro (shower of gold). It has far less cold tolerance than var. angustata and is killed outright rather than simply top-killed by hard freezes, so gardeners outside zone 9b-11 should treat it as an annual or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover. Prune after flowering flushes to maintain a tidy shrub form, since unpruned plants in tropical climates can grow leggy and tree-like within a few seasons.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)
